message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The study's structure is sound, and the cost arithmetic checks out:
- Vehicles: £990,000 over seven years is £141,400 a year.
- Crews: 12 operatives at £34,000 is £408,000.
- The total of £733,400 and the net cost of £490,400 are both correct.
- Every Table 1 rate matches its counts.

However, the study's two central conclusions are contradicted by its own figures:
- **"Participation held up across houses and flats."** Table 1 shows 66% for houses and 21% for flats.
- **"Fully funded."** The tonnage uses a participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot data, and Brookfield can't take the projected volume.

Corrected, the service is almost certainly not fully covered by the provisional allocation.

Since the service is a legal requirement, the question for Cabinet isn't whether to go ahead. It's whether the plan and the budget it approves are realistic. As written, they aren't.

## 1. Flats did not participate like houses

| Housing type | Participation | Kg per participating household per week |
|---|---|---|
| Houses | 66% | 1.9 |
| Flats | **21%** | 1.4 |

Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses and produced less waste per participating household. That is the opposite of "broadly similar".

The usual reasons are well known: flats have no space for an outdoor caddy, have shared bin stores, and offer less clear responsibility for putting caddies out. These typically need communal food-waste bins, different collection points and targeted communications. With about 10,400 flats in the district, a uniform service that ignores this will leave the flats' share of the service performing poorly. The study should set out a separate approach for flats and cost it. Communal bins for flats don't appear in Table 2.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the data

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate". The pilot overall was **57%**. The pilot's mix of houses and flats (80/20) matches the district's, so 57% transfers directly.

| Projection | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|
| As written (64%) | about 3,290 |
| Houses and flats separately | 2,713 + 159 = **about 2,870** |

The corrected figure is about 13% lower, so the disposal saving also falls, to about £212,500 a year, before the capacity problem below.

## 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year

Section 4 states Brookfield's contracted capacity is 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029, against a projection of about 2,870 tonnes, or 3,290 as written. That leaves roughly **1,070–1,490 tonnes a year with nowhere confirmed to go**. The study doesn't address this.

The options:
- **The plant 46 miles away.** This adds haulage time and vehicle mileage at a gate fee the study doesn't state. It may also require a transfer station or larger vehicles.
- **Incinerating the excess.** This saves nothing. It would also defeat the purpose of separate collection, and probably conflicts with the requirement that separately collected food waste be recycled. Check this with legal or policy colleagues.

So "treatment is local" holds for only about two-thirds of the tonnage.

## 4. Corrected, the service is not fully funded

| Scenario | Annual saving | Net cost | Against £520,000 allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As written: 3,290 t, all to Brookfield | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 headroom |
| Corrected tonnage, all diverted at £74/t | £212,500 | **£520,900** | already about £900 short |
| Corrected tonnage, only 1,800 t saves money | £133,200 | **£600,200** | about **£80,000 short** |

Even the most favourable corrected figure assumes the overflow tonnage costs nothing extra to haul 46 miles. The study must also add the following costs:
- **Crew on-costs.** Is £34,000 a salary or the full cost of employing someone? Employer's National Insurance and pension typically add 25–30%. On £408,000, that would be over £100,000.
- **Cover.** There's no allowance for leave and sickness cover, and no spare vehicle for a fleet of six.
- **Supervision, depot space** and the cost of financing the vehicles. Table 2 shows depreciation only, not interest.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in Section 6.
- **Communal bins for flats** (see section 1).

The £520,000 is also **provisional**, and the study doesn't say how long it lasts. Presenting a cost covered by a provisional allocation as "fully funded" is too strong even on the study's own figures.

## 5. Other points to check

- **Liners.** The pilot gave out "a supply" of liners, while the roll-out gives three months' worth. If pilot households had liners throughout, participation may fall once the roll-out supply runs out. Clarify whether liners continue, and whether that cost is in the £88,000.
- **Pilot effect.** Pilot residents knew they were being monitored and received extra attention. District-wide participation in the first year may be lower.
- **Timetable.** Vehicles arrive in March for a 5 April start, leaving almost no room for a delivery delay. Have a contingency, such as hiring vehicles.
- **Statutory deadline.** Most councils in England had to introduce weekly food waste collection by 31 March 2026. Confirm that April 2027 falls within an agreed transitional arrangement, and say so in the paper.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet

1. Remove the "broadly similar" claim, and add and cost a separate approach for flats.
2. Recompute tonnage with the participation rates for houses and flats separately (about 2,870 tonnes).
3. Set out how the tonnage beyond Brookfield's 1,800 tonnes will be treated, at what gate fee and haulage cost, until 2029.
4. Complete Table 2 with on-costs, cover, a spare vehicle, supervision, the cost of financing the vehicles, the phone line and the flats' containers.
5. Present the net cost as a range against the provisional allocation, and state any funding gap.
6. It's reasonable to recommend approving the vehicle order now, given the lead time. But ask Cabinet to confirm the fleet size once the treatment arrangements and flats approach are settled. The overflow route and the flats service may change the routing and the number of vehicles needed.

The honest summary is that the pilot shows houses take to the service well, and flats need a different approach. Treatment capacity covers about two-thirds of the expected tonnage. The net cost likely exceeds the provisional allocation once costs are complete, so the budget should plan for a gap.
